meta.title: Who really said "There is a land of the living and a land of the dead, and the bridge is love, the only survival, the only meaning"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Genuine. It is the closing sentence of Thornton Wilder’s 1927 novel The Bridge of San Luis Rey — the Abbess’s last thought, not a Wilder aphorism.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'There is a land of the living and a land of the dead, and the bridge is love, the only survival, the only meaning'?
meta.ogDescription: Wilder really wrote it. It ends The Bridge of San Luis Rey (1927) — and the printed text carries no comma after ‘dead’.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: It is the last sentence of The Bridge of San Luis Rey, Wilder’s second novel, first published in 1927 by Albert & Charles Boni — the closing words of Part Five, “Perhaps an Intention.” Confirmed in the full text of a Charles Boni printing of the 1927 edition; note that the printed line runs “…a land of the dead and the bridge is love…” with no comma after “dead.”

source.heading: The closing lines of the novel

docMeta.dd: The Bridge of San Luis Rey
Part Five, “Perhaps an Intention” — the novel’s final sentence
Madre María del Pilar, the Abbess — an unspoken thought, not narration

source.excerpt: “Even now,” she thought, “almost no one remembers Esteban and Pepita, but myself. Camila alone remembers her Uncle Pio and her son; this woman, her mother. But soon we shall die and all memory of those five will have left the earth, and we ourselves shall be loved for a while and forgotten. But the love will have been enough; all those impulses of love return to the love that made them. Even memory is not necessary for love. There is a land of the living and a land of the dead and the bridge is love, the only survival, the only meaning.”
trail: Wikiquote’s Thornton Wilder page ↗ carries the sentence in its list of quotations sourced to The Bridge of San Luis Rey (1927) — it is not flagged as disputed or misattributed.
The Thornton Wilder Society’s page for the work ↗ prints the whole closing paragraph and identifies it as the Abbess’s closing reflection.

The full text of a Charles Boni printing digitised by the Internet Archive ↗ carries the copyright line “THE BRIDGE OF SAN LUIS REY, COPYRIGHT, 1927 ALBERT & CHARLES BONI, INC.” and ends Part Five with the sentence exactly as quoted.

The NEA Big Read guide to the novel ↗ records that British Prime Minister Tony Blair read from the book’s closing lines at a memorial service for British victims of the World Trade Center attack after 11 September 2001.
source.excerptNote: The whole paragraph passes through the Abbess’s mind while she is speaking to two grieving women in her hospital. The final sentence is the last line of the book.

author.name: Thornton Wilder
author.heading: Thornton Wilder
author.bio: Thornton Niven Wilder (17 April 1897 – 7 December 1975) was an American novelist and playwright, and the only writer to win the Pulitzer Prize for both fiction and drama. The Bridge of San Luis Rey took the 1928 Pulitzer Prize for the Novel; Our Town (1938) and The Skin of Our Teeth (1943) each took the prize for drama. His recurring subject is ordinary life looked at from the far side of death — which is exactly the vantage this sentence speaks from.

misattribution.heading: The name is right — the label around it usually isn’t
misattribution.intro: This is one of the rare famous lines that survives checking intact. What goes wrong is everything bolted on around it: which book, whose voice, and one stray comma.

items.why: Wilder’s best-known title pulls the line towards itself. A-Z Quotes lists the sentence on its “Our Town” topic page ↗; its own source note credits The Bridge of San Luis Rey but dates it to a 1962 Limited Editions Club printing rather than the 1927 first edition.
It is a line of fiction, not an authorial maxim. The Thornton Wilder Society ↗ presents the paragraph as the Abbess’s closing reflection, and Wikipedia ↗ names her Madre María del Pilar.

Most circulating copies insert a comma after “dead.” The scanned Boni text ↗ has none, and neither do Wikiquote, the Wilder Society or the NEA guide. A small thing — but it is the tell that a copy has passed through a quote site rather than a book.

misattribution.truthLine: The sentence is genuine and verbatim — it is the last line of The Bridge of San Luis Rey (1927), thought rather than spoken, by the Abbess. See Wikiquote’s sourced list ↗.

context.heading: Why the line lands where it does
lead: The novel opens on a disaster and spends itself trying to justify one. “On Friday noon, July the twentieth, 1714, the finest bridge in all Peru broke and precipitated five travelers into the gulf below,” it begins — and a Franciscan, Brother Juniper, sets out to prove by investigation that the five deaths were designed rather than random. Wilder titles his first part “Perhaps an Accident” and his last “Perhaps an Intention,” and never quite closes the gap between them.

What he offers instead is this sentence, which arrives without argument in the mind of a woman who has buried people and gone on working. That is why it reads as consolation rather than doctrine: it is not the answer Brother Juniper was hunting, it is what is left standing when the hunt fails. The novel took the 1928 Pulitzer Prize for the Novel ↗, the first of Wilder’s three Pulitzers.
detailsBody: The NEA Big Read guide ↗ notes that Tony Blair read from the closing lines at a memorial service for British victims of the World Trade Center attack in the wake of 11 September 2001 — which is where a great many people first met the sentence, detached from the book that ends with it.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote's Thornton Wilder page lists "There is a land of the living and a land of the dead and the bridge is love, the only survival, the only meaning" under The Bridge of San Luis Rey (1927), with no Disputed or Misattributed flag.

The Thornton Wilder Society's page for the work prints the full closing paragraph ending "...There is a land of the living and a land of the dead and the bridge is love, the only survival, the only meaning," and describes it as the Abbess's closing reflection in the novel's final section.

The NEA Big Read guide states the novel was published in 1927, was awarded the Pulitzer Prize in 1928, and that "In the wake of the terrorist attacks on September 11, 2001, British Prime Minister Tony Blair read from The Bridge's closing lines at a memorial service for British victims of the World Trade Center attack," quoting the sentence without a comma after "dead."
The Internet Archive item is a freely readable scan of The Bridge of San Luis Rey dated 1927, offering full-text download and not lending-restricted.

The full OCR text of that Internet Archive item carries the copyright line "THE BRIDGE OF SAN LUIS REY, COPYRIGHT, 1927 ALBERT & CHARLES BONI, INC.", opens Part One with "On Friday noon, July the twentieth, 1714, the finest bridge in all Peru broke and precipitated five travelers into the gulf below," and ends Part Five ("Perhaps an Intention") with "There is a land of the living and a land of the dead and the bridge is love, the only survival, the only meaning." — no comma after "dead."

Wikipedia's article on the novel gives first publication 1927 by Albert & Charles Boni, the 1928 Pulitzer, names the Abbess Madre María del Pilar, quotes the closing line without a comma after "dead," and records Tony Blair quoting it at a September 11 memorial service in 2001.

Wikipedia's article on Thornton Wilder gives his dates as 17 April 1897 – 7 December 1975, describes him as an American playwright and novelist, and lists Pulitzer Prizes in 1928 (Novel, The Bridge of San Luis Rey), 1938 (Drama, Our Town) and 1943 (Drama, The Skin of Our Teeth).

A-Z Quotes lists the sentence on its "Our Town" topic page, attributed to Thornton Wilder, with a source note reading "Thornton Wilder (1962). 'The Bridge of San Luis Rey', New York : Limited Editions Club" — dating it to a 1962 reprint rather than the 1927 first edition.
